idiom_name: envelope struct with json.RawMessage deferred decode plus switch on the wire type
implementation_notes: encoding/json's documented approach to polymorphism is an envelope struct that captures the discriminator and keeps the payload as json.RawMessage, followed by a switch that unmarshals the raw bytes into the concrete source struct and maps it to the canonical struct - the standard library parses, Go's switch routes, and one plain function per format replaces the Translator objects. A map[string]func(json.RawMessage) (Canonical, error) built at start-up plays the registry, and fmt.Errorf with %w (or errors.Join) keeps per-format failures traceable; XML partners go through encoding/xml with exactly the same shape. Interfaces plus structs are still justified when translators need injected dependencies (a client, a clock, lookup tables) or when detection is heuristic rather than tag-based.
pitfalls: json.Unmarshal ignores unknown fields by default, so a renamed partner field silently becomes the zero value; use Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields (or validate after mapping) when the canonical contract must be closed.
Decoding into float64 loses precision for money and 64-bit ids: use json.Number or a string-typed canonical field, and be explicit about int64 in interface{} payloads.

json.RawMessage only defers the copy - the slice aliases the input buffer, so an in-place transformation mutates the caller's bytes; clone it when the raw payload is retained or sent to an invalid-message channel.
encoding/xml matches element names case-sensitively and ignores namespaces in struct tags, so partner XML that looks identical but differs in namespace silently maps to zero values.
